result: After exposure to motion sequences, presenting only the first or last stimulus (start-only or end-only trials) elicited time-locked elevated neural responses during periods corresponding to the missing stimuli, though no peak was observed for the final interval. These cue-triggered elevated responses resembled those from full sequence trials.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding, with one reviewer stating 'Identifying the two types of activation after exposure to a sequence of motion directions is very interesting' and another noting that 'showing either the starting movement direction, or ending movement direction causes a coarse-grained brain response that is similar to that elicited by the complete sequence.' The experimental design and analyses were described as 'solid.'

result: While motion direction information could be decoded in full sequence trials and for the cue stimulus in start/end-only trials, subsequent motion direction information was absent at the group level during the post-cue blank period. This indicates the cue-triggered elevated response was not consistently feature-specific across participants and trials.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding, with one explicitly noting 'they show by decoding the sensor responses that this brain activity actually does not carry information about the actual sequence and the motion directions, at least not on the time scale of the initial sequence.' The editor described the evidence as 'convincing evidence for both feature-specific and non-specific sequence representations.'

result: Using temporally delayed linear modeling (TDLM), backward replay of the exposed motion sequence was detected during the post-cue blank period in both start-only and end-only conditions, with peak transition lags at 28-40 ms. The replayed sequence was approximately 10 times faster than the evoked activity sequence, and only backward replay was detected when examining all potential sequences.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this finding as a key contribution. One reviewer stated 'They also show a reverse reply on a highly-compressed time scale, which is elicited during the period of elevated activity.' The editor described this as 'convincing evidence' and noted that 'finding such replays in humans is novel.' The statistical methodology was deemed 'valid' though complex.

result: In Experiment 2, when the second or third stimulus (rather than first or last) was presented as a cue, no evidence of forward or backward replay was found in either condition.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this control experiment finding without challenge. One reviewer noted that replay was 'activated by the first and last elements of the sequence, but not others,' implicitly affirming the Experiment 2 results. This finding supports the boundary-sensitivity interpretation of replay.

result: In Experiment 3 with brief exposure (no pre-exposure phase), a numerical trend of backward replay was found in the start-only condition (not reaching significance), while the end-only condition just reached significance. This suggests even brief exposure can induce a trend for backward replay.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as part of the overall pattern of results. One reviewer noted the findings are 'interesting and novel,' and the experimental procedures were described as 'solid.' The claim about brief exposure inducing replay trends aligns with the reviewers' acceptance of the broader replay findings.

result: Replay events were associated with transient ripple power increases at 120-180 Hz localized to bilateral visual cortex. Critically, the right MTL (including hippocampus and amygdala) showed power increases 30 ms prior to visual cortex activation, suggesting information flow from MTL to visual cortex.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding. One reviewer stated 'The finding that activity in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) preceded that in the visual cortex suggests that the visual cortex may serve as a platform for the manifestation of replay events.' Another noted 'these replays seem to occur during periods of cortical ripples, similar to what is found in animal studies.' The sophisticated MEG analyses were deemed convincing.

result: Visual sequence exposure induces twofold brain plasticity: time-locked, non-feature-specific elevated responses and non-time-locked, feature-specific backward replay that occurs in a time-compressed manner and can only be triggered by the first or last stimulus of the sequence.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly supported this overarching finding. The editor described it as a 'valuable study' with 'convincing evidence for both feature-specific and non-specific sequence representations.' One reviewer stated 'Identifying the two types of activation after exposure to a sequence of motion directions is very interesting' and that 'The findings are interesting and novel.' The distinction between the two types of plasticity was central to reviewers' positive assessment.

result: Unlike expectation-based responses in static contexts which are feature-specific, prediction-related elevated responses in dynamic temporal contexts are not feature-specific, potentially facilitating general processing of any upcoming stimuli rather than stimuli with specific features.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interpretation as part of the study's contribution. One reviewer noted the study 'shows that this brain activity actually does not carry information about the actual sequence and the motion directions,' supporting the non-feature-specific nature. The editor's description of 'non-specific sequence representations' as a key finding affirms this claim.

result: Contrary to prevailing notions that replay requires lengthy training, even brief exposure to a visual sequence is sufficient to induce replay, which may play a critical role in memorizing the visual sequence.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as novel and important. One reviewer stated the findings are 'interesting and novel,' and the editor noted that 'finding such replays in humans is novel.' The experimental evidence from Experiment 3 showing replay trends with brief exposure supports this claim, and reviewers raised no objections to this interpretation.

result: The non-feature-specific elevated responses could be induced by rhythmic entrainment, where rhythmic presentation of the motion sequence entrains oscillatory activity leading to periodic activation of sensory cortices, serving as a mechanism for general facilitation of neural processing independent of specific stimulus features.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this mechanistic interpretation. While speculative, it is presented as a plausible explanation supported by prior literature. The reviewers' acceptance of the non-feature-specific nature of elevated responses and their description of the experimental design and analyses as 'solid' implicitly supports this mechanistic account.

result: Feature-specific replay operates through a different mechanism driven by intrinsic neural processes rather than direct external stimuli, manifesting spontaneously rather than time-locked to stimulus onset, and may facilitate integration of fragmented experiences into coherent representations for visual sequence learning and memory.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interpretation. One reviewer initially questioned 'why the second type of activation was suggested to occur spontaneously' but noted 'this concern has been satisfactorily addressed in the revision,' indicating the authors successfully clarified the spontaneous, non-time-locked nature of replay. The mechanistic distinction between the two types of plasticity was central to reviewers' positive evaluation.

result: Replay events are likely initiated by the hippocampus and involve active communication between the hippocampus and visual cortex, with the hippocampus encoding relationships among stimuli while visual cortex acts as a platform for manifestation of replay events.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this interpretation. One reviewer stated 'The finding that activity in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) preceded that in the visual cortex suggests that the visual cortex may serve as a platform for the manifestation of replay events, which potentially enhance visual sequence learning.' The temporal precedence finding (C48-C50) provides empirical support for this mechanistic claim.
